title: Yields Ease, Jobs Cool, Micron Surges
summary: US equities reached fresh highs as yields and oil eased, but bond-market risks remain central for UK investors. This week also covers softer US payrolls, revised UK growth, Micron’s exceptional AI-memory results, Nike’s early-stage turnaround, and the key events ahead.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: US markets hit fresh highs as yields and oil eased — but the bond-market warning light is not off.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Welcome to The Weekly Market Brief, covering Tuesday the twenty-ninth of September to Tuesday the sixth of October. As ever, this is general information, not personal financial advice. Do your own research.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And maybe keep one hand on the desk. The tape looked calmer by Tuesday, but underneath it was still twitchy.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Top story first: US equities rebounded, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq at records, helped by lower Treasury yields, lower oil, and continuing AI optimism.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, but earlier in the week, global bond selling had pushed US Treasury yields to multi-decade highs before they reversed intraday. That matters for UK investors as well.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Because long yields touch almost everything: equity valuations, bond funds, mortgages, and property-sensitive sectors.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Lower yields can support growth and technology shares. But if long yields move higher again, that’s a headwind for equity multiples and duration-heavy bond funds.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the Bank of England added a UK-specific warning.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Its Financial Policy Committee said gilt and US Treasury yields had reached levels not seen since 2008. Adjustments had mostly been gradual, but hedge-fund leverage in gilts remained elevated.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So even with indices rising, there’s still a financial-stability undertone.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That’s the bit people miss. A rising index doesn’t mean the plumbing is boring. [chuckles]

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Second story: US labour cooled sharply. September nonfarm payrolls rose just twenty-nine thousand, and unemployment was four point two percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And July and August payrolls were revised down by sixty thousand combined. Average hourly earnings rose zero point one percent month on month, and three percent year on year.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That helps explain why markets became more comfortable with no Fed hike in October.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, but it’s two-sided. Softer jobs data helps rate-sensitive assets only if it doesn’t become an earnings recession. Banks, staffing, discretionary retail, travel and semiconductors are the areas to watch.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Third: the UK data looked a little better, though not enough to remove the bigger concerns.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: ONS revised Q2 real GDP growth to zero point five percent, after zero point six percent in Q1. Real household disposable income per head rose one percent.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the underlying current-account deficit, excluding precious metals, narrowed to eleven point three billion pounds, or one point four percent of GDP.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Helpful for sterling-risk perceptions, yes. But not enough, on its own, to make fiscal and gilt-market worries vanish.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Earnings. The standout was Micron.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Standout is doing some work there. Fiscal Q4 revenue was fifty-four point two three billion dollars, up from forty-one point four six billion in fiscal Q3 and eleven point three two billion a year earlier.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: GAAP net income was thirty-seven point seven billion dollars, and GAAP gross margin was eighty-six point eight percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue to sixty-one point five billion dollars, plus or minus one point five billion. That’s powerful evidence that AI demand is feeding into memory pricing.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So Micron is one to research further, not a recommendation — and the obvious risk is cyclicality.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Very. What would change my mind? Evidence of HBM or DRAM oversupply, hyperscaler capex discipline, customer concentration problems, or margins normalising faster than expected.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The other big earnings story is Nike, where the turnaround still looks early and messy. Fiscal Q1 revenue was eleven point two billion dollars, down four percent reported.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Gross margin improved sixty basis points to forty-two point eight percent, but net income fell two percent. That’s not a clean growth story.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And for fiscal 2027, Nike expects revenue to decline high single digits, with adjusted diluted EPS of one dollar fifteen to one dollar thirty-five.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The risk is that investors focus on savings. The case needs product momentum, healthier channels and China stabilisation — not just a tidier cost base.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Week ahead. Wednesday at seven p.m. UK time, Fed minutes. Thursday, PepsiCo releases Q3 materials at eleven a.m., with Q&A at one fifteen. Also Thursday, Tesco reports interims.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And Friday at three p.m., Delta Air Lines’ September-quarter webcast gives read-throughs on oil, premium travel, corporate demand and free cash flow.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That’s it for this week. Links and the full written briefing are in the show notes. Reminder: this has been general market information, not personal financial advice. Do your own research, and we’ll be back next week.
